analysis.one_liner: Caps ocean shipping rates between the mainland and Hawaii, Alaska, and Puerto Rico.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a hearing or a vote: it was referred to a House subcommittee and died when the 116th Congress ended, with no cosponsors.
analysis.plain_summary: Goods shipped by sea between the mainland and Hawaii, Alaska, and Puerto Rico are carried under a federal law (the Jones Act) that requires American-built, American-flagged, American-crewed ships, which makes those rates far higher than comparable international shipping. This bill would say a shipping rate in that trade is 'reasonable' — and thus legal — only if it comes within 10% of a comparable international shipping rate index recognized by the Federal Maritime Commission. In practice, it would force domestic carriers to charge prices closer to what the rest of the world pays, lowering shipping costs that get passed into consumer prices in those states and territories.
analysis.who_benefits: Consumers and businesses in Hawaii, Alaska, Puerto Rico, and other noncontiguous U.S. territories, who pay higher prices for nearly everything shipped in by sea because domestic ocean rates run well above international ones. Local importers, retailers, and farmers who pay freight as an input cost would also gain, since a lower shipping benchmark would feed through to their costs.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Consumers in Hawaii, Alaska, and Puerto Rico

how_it_helps.text: Defines a 'reasonable rate' for noncontiguous domestic ocean shipping as one within 10% of a comparable international ocean rate index recognized by the Federal Maritime Commission, capping how far above world rates carriers can charge [S2][S3].

Because almost all consumer goods reaching Hawaii, Alaska, and Puerto Rico arrive by ship, freight rates are embedded in local prices; a cap on shipping rates would lower the cost of everyday goods for residents of those places [S2].

analysis.who_pays: U.S.-flag ocean carriers serving the Hawaii, Alaska, and Puerto Rico trades, which currently charge rates well above international benchmarks and would lose that revenue margin. Any carrier whose costs genuinely exceed the index because of Jones Act crewing and U.S.-build requirements could face unprofitable routes.

drawbacks.text: A cap pegged to an international rate index may not cover the higher cost of operating U.S.-built, U.S.-crewed vessels required by the Jones Act, which could squeeze carriers on routes where no cheaper substitute exists [S3].

If the 10% band or the index chosen by the Federal Maritime Commission proved too tight, carriers could reduce service frequency or exit routes, and the bill leaves the choice of a 'comparable' index largely to the agency's discretion [S2][S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is real and concentrated where the need is: island and territory residents pay a shipping premium on essentially everything they buy, and tying 'reasonable' to an international index attacks that premium directly. The honest objection is that the premium partly reflects the Jones Act's requirement for costlier U.S.-built and U.S.-crewed ships, so a rate cap without touching that underlying law risks either squeezing carriers or being challenged as arbitrary. But the bill is narrow and leaves flexibility to the Federal Maritime Commission, so the main problem with it is that it was never actually considered.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Transportation and Infrastructure Committee and then to its Coast Guard and Maritime Transportation Subcommittee, where it sat without a hearing or a vote until the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Ed Case introduced the bill on December 19, 2019, and it was referred to the House Committee on Transportation and Infrastructure [S1][S5].
The next day it was referred to the Subcommittee on Coast Guard and Maritime Transportation, where no further action was taken for the rest of the 116th Congress [S5].
No other member cosponsored the bill, and it never received a hearing, a markup, or a floor vote [S4][S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: U.S.-flag ocean carriers in the noncontiguous trades are better off, since they continue charging rates without any cap tied to international benchmarks. Consumers in Hawaii, Alaska, and Puerto Rico gained nothing because the bill never moved.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: U.S.-flag shipping carriers serving the islands

for.name: Ed Case
for.what_they_did: Sponsored the bill and introduced it in the House; it was his lone-authored measure with introductory remarks in the Congressional Record.

against.name: House Transportation and Infrastructure Committee
against.what_they_did: Referred the bill to its Coast Guard and Maritime Transportation Subcommittee and never scheduled a hearing or markup.

sides.party_line_note: No votes ever occurred and no other member of either party cosponsored, so the partisan shape cannot be measured; the only recorded support was from a single Hawaii Democrat [S4][S5].

industries.industry: U.S.-flag domestic ocean carriers (Jones Act noncontiguous trades)
industries.note: These carriers charge rates well above comparable international shipping because the Jones Act requires U.S.-built, U.S.-flagged, U.S.-crewed vessels with no foreign competition on domestic routes; the bill would cap their rates within 10% of an international index, directly cutting their revenue margin. Their existing advantage is the public's cost, since the excess freight is embedded in prices for goods in Hawaii, Alaska, and Puerto Rico.

industries.industry: Importers, retailers, and producers in Hawaii, Alaska, and Puerto Rico
industries.note: These businesses pay ocean freight on nearly everything they sell or use, so a rate benchmark tied to international levels would lower their input costs and pass through to local consumers.
